title: Resiliency Architecture
objective: By the end of this lesson you can choose high-availability patterns, compare RAID levels, design a backup scheme, and match recovery sites to cost and speed.

blocks.text: High availability (HA) removes single points of failure through redundancy: clustered servers, multiple power feeds, paired network paths. Fault tolerance goes further, letting a system keep working through a component failure with service intact. Graceful degradation means a system sheds features but keeps core service alive.

items: Redundancy: duplicates of a critical part, active or standby.
Clustering: several nodes acting as one service; failover moves work to a survivor.
NIC teaming: multiple network cards as one logical link.
UPS and generators: bridge short and long power loss.
Load balancing: spreads work and health-checks members out of rotation.

blocks.title: RAID is availability, and RAID is a backup for no one
blocks.text: RAID keeps a system running through disk failure. It does nothing against deletion, ransomware, or fire, because the array faithfully copies every change. Backups answer those.

rows: Changes since the last backup of any type

blocks.text: The 3-2-1 rule is the exam's default backup design: three copies of the data, on two different media, with one copy off-site or offline. Snapshots capture a point-in-time state for quick rollback, and immutable or air-gapped copies resist ransomware that hunts reachable backups.

blocks.title: Design resiliency for one service
steps: Service: an internal wiki used during business hours; tolerated downtime is four hours.
Pick a site type and justify it.
Pick a backup scheme (types plus the 3-2-1 rule) and name the restore order after a ransomware event.
Pick one HA measure inside the primary site.
blocks.expected: Warm site fits a four-hour window. Scheme: weekly full plus daily incremental, one copy off-site or immutable; restore the last full, then incrementals to the latest clean point. HA measure: clustered virtual machines or at least a standby node with shared storage.

cheatsheet: HA removes single points of failure; fault tolerance survives failure without service loss; graceful degradation keeps core service.
RAID 0 none, RAID 1 mirror, RAID 5 one parity drive, RAID 6 two, RAID 10 mirrors striped. RAID is availability, never a backup.
Full copies all; incremental copies since the last backup; differential copies since the last full.
3-2-1: three copies, two media, one off-site; immutability or air gaps defend backups from ransomware.
Sites: hot = ready now, warm = equipped, cold = shell; cost falls as speed falls.

checkpoint.prompt: After a crypto-virus event, the backup repository attached to the network was encrypted along with production. Which design change best addresses this?

choices.C: Keep one backup copy offline or immutable
choices.D: Add a second network card to the backup server

checkpoint.explanation: Ransomware encrypts every reachable copy, so an offline or immutable copy is the fix. RAID and NIC changes address hardware failure, and the full-versus-incremental choice does not change reachability.

checkpoint.prompt: Which backup scheme restores with the fewest pieces after a complete loss on Friday, assuming daily backups since Sunday's full?
checkpoint.explanation: A differential accumulates all changes since the full, so Friday's restore needs the full plus Friday's differential alone. Incrementals need every day in sequence.
